about: Facts for stone's print-failure physics (failsim.py): convection, melt viscosity, bed adhesion and the Creality K2 profile, each with its source. A value with an assumption field is a modeling choice, not a measurement. Entries with copy_of repeat Track S's materials.json and Track T's slicer.json, citations and all, until those files are on main; failsim reads the originals first.

entries.note: Standard gravity; weight of strands, beads and parts.
entries.quote: It is a constant defined by ISO standard 80000 as 9.80665 m/s2
entries.source: Wikipedia, Standard gravity

entries.note: Convection from a bead in still air (fan off). The same paper cools its PLA beads with a lumped Newton model, as stone does.
entries.quote: Convective heat Transfer coefficient h 10 W·m−2K−1 Natural convection of air
entries.source: He, Zhu, Zhang, Yang, Investigation on Bridging Defects in 3D-Printed Polylactic Acid Beams Using Fused Filament Fabrication, Polymers 2026, 18(2), 261, Table 3

entries.note: PLA thermal conductivity, same table; used only to check the bead is thin enough for a lumped model (Biot number).
entries.source: He, Zhu, Zhang, Yang, Investigation on Bridging Defects in 3D-Printed Polylactic Acid Beams Using Fused Filament Fabrication, Polymers 2026, 18(2), 261, Table 3

entries.note: PLA specific heat for the lumped bead cooling.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985
entries.cite: Materials 2020 13:4985 PLA and ABS thermal model

entries.note: ABS conductivity and specific heat by temperature (their Table 5, from Zhou et al.). stone averages cp from Tg up to the nozzle temperature. PETG has no sourced pair here: stone uses PLA's and says so.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985

entries.note: Dry air at 400 K (127 C), the film temperature between a fresh bead and the chamber air, for the fan-on convection.
entries.source: Engineering ToolBox, Air: thermophysical properties

entries.note: Forced convection across a cylinder for Re Pr > 0.2: the bead in the part-cooling fan's air. h = Nu k / d.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Churchill-Bernstein equation

entries.note: Air speed over the bead with the part fan at full speed. No maker publishes it.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Part-cooling air speed at the nozzle, 2 to 10 m/s; 5 used. It sets the fan-on h and so how long a bead stays soft.

entries.note: PLA melt viscosity by temperature and shear rate: eta0 = D1 exp(-A1 (T - T*) / (A2 + T - T*)), eta = eta0 / (1 + (eta0 rate / tau*)^(1 - n)). Fitted to NatureWorks Ingeo 3251D, an injection grade; filament PLA is close but not the same. PETG and ABS have no sourced fit: stone uses PLA's and says so.
entries.quote: Table 2 Data-fitted Cross-WLF parameters of the PLA 3251D. A1 16.71 A2 (K) 51.60 D1 (Pa*s) 2.045 × 10^7 D3 (K/Pa) 0 T* (K) 373.15 n 0.3846 τ* (Pa) 1.29 × 10^5
entries.source: Pricci, Physics-Based Predictive Modeling of Gravity-Induced Sagging in Support-Free Pellet Additive Manufacturing, Polymers 2025, 17(21), 2858, Table 2

entries.note: A viscous beam bends like an elastic one with E replaced by 3 eta and deflection by its rate: stone's soft-bead droop.
entries.quote: For a Newtonian Fluid, the Trouton ratio equals three.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Extensional viscosity

entries.note: Tensile pull-off strength of PLA printed on aluminum, over their 16 treatments and bed temperatures; stone uses the lowest for the tip check (force over the whole footprint). No paper measured PEI or glass this way; treated aluminum stands in.
entries.quote: The highest tensile adhesion strength was obtained with acid etching at 65 °C (1.71 MPa) ... The lowest value was recorded for acid etching at 85 °C (0.40 MPa)
entries.source: Campos-Jurado, Rodriguez-Alabanda, Guerrero-Vacas, Manufacturing of Polymer-Metal Composite by Fused Filament Fabrication: Adhesion of PLA and PETG on Aluminum, Polymers 2025, 17(16), 2210
entries.cite: Polymers 2025 17:2210 PLA and PETG on aluminum

entries.note: Lap-shear strength of the same PLA on aluminum; the lowest is used for the slide check.
entries.quote: For PLA, the highest shear adhesion strength was obtained with acid etching at 65 °C (3.92 MPa) ... dropping to a minimum of 0.52 MPa (fine sanding, 85 °C)
entries.source: Campos-Jurado, Rodriguez-Alabanda, Guerrero-Vacas, Manufacturing of Polymer-Metal Composite by Fused Filament Fabrication: Adhesion of PLA and PETG on Aluminum, Polymers 2025, 17(16), 2210
entries.cite: Polymers 2025 17:2210 PLA and PETG on aluminum

entries.note: Peak 90 degree peel force of a printed PLA strip on borosilicate glass (DIN EN 28510-1 style test). On Pertinax PLA peaked at 160 N. stone turns the peak into an edge stress with Hetenyi's beam on an elastic foundation (failsim.hetenyi).
entries.quote: The maximum was measured for PLA with a value of 231 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: Polypropylene, a low surface energy plastic, on the same glass (about 4 N) and Pertinax (7.8 N maximum). Its ratio to PLA is stone's dirty-plate factor.
entries.quote: The adhesion forces for the material pairing PP - borosilicate glass are about 4 N ... The maximum adhesion force was measured for PLA with a value of 160 N while polypropylene (PP) only adheres with a maximum of 7.8 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: PETG (Filamentworld) on borosilicate glass, average of the peak forces.
entries.quote: PETG has an adhesion force between 94 N and 107 N with an average of 102 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: Width and thickness of the peeled strip. The paper prints at 0.5 mm layers with a 1 mm nozzle; the strip size is only in its Fig. 52.
entries.quote: nozzle diameter 1.0 mm, filament diameter 1.75 mm, layer height and first layer height 0.5 mm
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)
entries.assumption: Strip 25 mm wide (the width of an ISO 8510-1 / DIN EN 28510-1 peel specimen) and one 0.5 mm layer thick.

entries.note: Dirty-plate factor: a plate with skin oil or dust holds the part the way a poorly wetting plastic holds a clean plate. Computed from the peel data: PP / PLA = 4 / 231 = 0.017 on glass, 7.8 / 160 = 0.049 on Pertinax. stone uses the milder 0.049, so a dirty plate that fails at 0.049 fails at 0.017 too.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)
entries.assumption: A contaminated plate keeps the same fraction of its hold as PP keeps of PLA's on a clean plate.

entries.value: end of a long beam on an elastic foundation: y = 2 P lambda / k under an end force P, y = 2 M0 lambda^2 / k under an end moment M0, lambda = (k / 4EI)^(1/4)
entries.note: The first layer is the foundation (k = E b / t1 per unit length, E of the part itself); the stack above it is the beam. Edge peel stress = k y / b. For a peel strip of width b and thickness h pulled at its end: sigma = 2 P lambda / b. For a stack of n layers of t: sigma = sqrt(3 n) sigma_l (see failsim.warp_rule). The OCR of the scan is cleaned up in the quote.
entries.quote: Concentrated Force at One End ... Deflections at the end points: y = (2Pλ/k) (Sinh λl Cosh λl − sin λl cos λl) / (Sinh² λl − sin² λl) ... Concentrated Moment at One End ... y = (2M0λ²/k) (Sinh² λl + sin² λl) / (Sinh² λl − sin² λl) ... λ = ⁴√(k/4EI)
entries.source: M. Hetenyi, Beams on Elastic Foundation (1946), archive.org scan, eqs. 39 and 40 (finite beam, free ends; both reduce to the long-beam values when lambda l is large)

entries.value: sigma_edge = sqrt(3 n) x alpha x integral of E(T) dT from T_part to Tg
entries.note: Each layer bonds stress-free at Tg and cools to the part temperature (the bed's), so it carries sigma_l = alpha x integral E dT, read on the measured stiffness-vs-temperature curve. All n layers together pull with sigma_l H at mid-height while the bed holds the bottom: an end moment sigma_l H^2 / 2 per mm of edge. Hetenyi's end-moment formula with the first layer as the foundation gives sigma_edge = sqrt(3 H / t1) sigma_l = sqrt(3 n) sigma_l. The corner lifts when that passes the bond's edge strength: min(peel stress, the plastic's own Z strength) x the plate's cleanliness factor.
entries.source: stone model from failsim.hetenyi and materials data
entries.assumption: Solid part, no stress relaxation, long edge (Hetenyi's long-beam limit), part temperature = bed temperature: all make stone call a lift sooner than real prints show.

entries.note: Flat face of a 0.4 mm nozzle that drags over the top layer; the drag is the melt's shear stress on it.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: A 0.4 mm nozzle's flat tip is about 1.0 mm across.

entries.note: Friction of a soft strand on the bed or the part, in the falling-strand model.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Coulomb friction 0.5; it only changes how far a fallen strand slides, not whether it falls.

entries.note: Share of the plastic extruded with nothing under the nozzle that stays on the nozzle and heater block (blob_on_nozzle); the rest falls as strands.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Half of what is extruded into air stays on the nozzle.

entries.value: a = catenary constant with sag(L_usable) = one layer height
entries.note: A bridge strand hangs as a catenary z = a (cosh(x/a) - 1) with one constant a for the material: the one that sags exactly one layer at the slicer's usable bridge length (failsim.max_bridge_length). Longer spans sag more than a layer: the next layer has nothing to land on.
entries.source: stone model from failsim.max_bridge_length
entries.assumption: At the usable bridge length a bridge sags one layer height; the catenary constant is the same for every span.

entries.note: A ledge whose tip droops one layer height or more leaves the next layer nothing to print on (kind supports). Half a layer or more shows (kind droop): a line's rounded side already hides about half its height (OrcaSlicer's line is a rectangle with round ends).
entries.source: stone model
entries.assumption: Droop of one layer fails the ledge; half a layer is the smallest droop that shows.

entries.value: predict positions under gravity, project segment lengths, collide with the ground, apply friction, set velocity from the position change
entries.note: The falling strand: a chain of short segments solved by position based dynamics.
entries.source: Mueller, Heidelberger, Hennix, Ratcliff, Position Based Dynamics, Journal of Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2) 2007, 109-118
entries.cite: Mueller et al. 2007 Position Based Dynamics

entries.note: Measured from the bed: a face sloping less than 30 deg from horizontal (more than 60 deg from vertical) gets support. The Creality K2 0.20mm Standard profile keeps 30. stone turns it into a reach per layer: layer height x tan(60 deg), 0.35 mm at 0.2 mm layers.
entries.quote: Support will be generated for overhangs whose slope angle is below the threshold. The smaller this value is, the steeper the overhang that can be printed without support.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp, support_threshold_angle (default 30)

entries.note: A print profile setting, not a filament one: OrcaSlicer's K2 profiles use 10 mm for PLA and PETG alike. PETG bridges sag more than PLA in practice; stone keeps 10 mm for both and says so (assumption that the slicer's limit holds for PETG).
entries.quote: This is the maximum length of bridges that don't need support. Set it to 0 if you want all bridges to be supported, and set it to a very large value if you don't want any bridges to be supported.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp, max_bridge_length (default 10); resources/profiles/Creality/process/0.20mm Standard @Creality K2 0.4 nozzle.json (10)

entries.note: Line widths of the K2 0.20mm Standard profile, 0.4 mm nozzle.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer resources/profiles/Creality/process/0.20mm Standard @Creality K2 0.4 nozzle.json

entries.note: Print speeds of the K2 0.20mm Standard profile. The fastest of them (inner wall, 300 mm/s) is the max speed OrcaSlicer's auto brim uses.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer resources/profiles/Creality/process/0.20mm Standard @Creality K2 0.4 nozzle.json

entries.value: stable while the center of mass is over the support polygon
entries.note: A part standing on the bed stays up on its own only while its center of mass, seen from above, is inside the convex hull of its first layer. stone checks it for the part as printed so far, at every layer.
entries.quote: its support polygon is a horizontal region over which the center of mass must lie to achieve static stability. For example, for an object resting on a horizontal surface (e.g. a table), the support polygon is the convex hull of its "footprint" on the table.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Support polygon
